justification_text:
My point estimates reflected a view of modest stability with slight upward drift over time. At the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the prevailing price level, assuming minimal overnight movement and that short-term momentum or intraday positioning would keep the asset near its recent trading range. For the one-week estimate, I nudged the forecast marginally higher, acknowledging that any near-term catalyst or gradual mean-reversion tendency could produce a small positive drift without committing to a strong directional view. At the one-month horizon, the estimate continued drifting slightly higher, reflecting a baseline assumption of modest positive drift that is common in many financial assets over medium-term windows, balanced against the possibility of consolidation or mild correction.

The confidence interval widths widened progressively across horizons, which is a straightforward reflection of uncertainty compounding over time. At one day, the interval was relatively tight because short-term price dynamics tend to be more predictable and anchored by current market conditions. By one week, additional uncertainty from scheduled economic data releases, central bank communications, or shifts in market sentiment pushed the interval wider. At one month, the interval widened considerably further to capture a broader range of possible macroeconomic developments, earnings announcements, liquidity conditions, and longer-duration trend reversals that could materially alter the trajectory.

Several specific risks could push realized outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden deterioration in risk appetite — driven by geopolitical escalation, an unexpected credit event, or a sharper-than-anticipated tightening signal from a major central bank — could push prices well below the lower bound of even the one-month interval. Conversely, a strong positive surprise in economic data, a dovish policy pivot, or a short-squeeze dynamic could drive prices meaningfully above the upper bound. Liquidity conditions also matter: thin markets can amplify moves in either direction beyond what historical volatility would suggest.

It is also worth noting that my intervals were constructed assuming relatively normal market functioning. In tail-risk scenarios — such as a flash crash, a major institutional forced liquidation, or an unanticipated geopolitical shock — realized price movements could easily breach all three intervals simultaneously, particularly at the one-week and one-month horizons. These are low-probability but non-negligible events that any honest probabilistic forecast must acknowledge as genuine risks to the stated ranges.
